text:
### Observed differences

- In the earlier window, the six activities A33, A35, A36, A37, A38 and A39 each ran in every trace (200 of 200), once per case; in the later window each runs in only about 47–57 in 100 traces, still at most once per case [OCC001, OCC002, OCC003, OCC004, OCC005, OCC006].
- The six split into two tightly coupled groups, A33–A35–A36 and A37–A38–A39. In both windows the members of each group run together and in no fixed order among themselves; in the later window each group still co-occurs internally in about 46–56 in 100 traces, with neither member present in the remaining traces [REL013, REL014, REL018, REL025, REL026, REL027].
- The two groups became mutually exclusive. Earlier, every trace contained all six activities with the first group always before the second (co-occurrence 100 in 100; first-before-second about 98–100 in 100). In the later window, traces containing activities of both groups fell to about 2–3 in 100, while about 44 in 100 traces show only first-group activities and about 53 in 100 only second-group activities [REL015, REL016, REL017, REL019, REL020, REL021, REL022, REL023, REL024].
- A30 and A31 still appear in every trace in both windows; A30 still precedes whichever group runs and A31 still follows it [REL001, REL002, REL003, REL004, REL005, REL006, REL007, REL008, REL009, REL010, REL011, REL012].
- Routing changed accordingly. Earlier, A30's outgoing transitions went almost only to A33 (about 34%), A35 (about 36%) and A36 (about 29%); in the later window they spread across all six group activities (about 13–20% each) [DIR001]. A33, A35 and A36, which previously never led to A31, now lead to A31 in about 24–34% of their outgoing transitions, while their transitions to A37, A38 and A39 fell from about 8–14% to about 1% [DIR002, DIR003, DIR004].
- Event-position gaps compressed: the distance from A30 to A37/A38/A39 and from A33/A35/A36 to A31 was 4–5 positions earlier and is 1–3 positions in the later window [LAG001, LAG002, LAG003, LAG004, LAG007, LAG010]. Six further lag items rest on only 4–5 later-window observations and are not relied upon here [LAG005, LAG006, LAG008, LAG009, LAG011, LAG012].
- For scale: 49 control-flow items qualified, against roughly 0.75 expected by chance in an unchanged process [screening].

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports the hypothesis that the segment between A30 and A31 changed from two always-executed groups in sequence to a per-case choice between them: earlier every trace ran A30, then A33–A35–A36 together, then A37–A38–A39 together, then A31; in the later window a trace typically runs A30, then either the group A33–A35–A36 (about 44 in 100 cases) or the group A37–A38–A39 (about 53 in 100), then A31 — so each case now skips one of the two groups. This is a participation and routing change (a group is skipped), not a shift of shares between always-present alternatives. It rests on direct relational evidence of exclusivity, the halved participation of all six activities, the new A30-to-second-group and first-group-to-A31 transitions, and the compressed positional gaps; the qualified-item count (49 versus about 0.75 expected) exceeds what chance re-splits produce by orders of magnitude [REL015, REL022, OCC001, OCC004, DIR001, DIR002, LAG001, LAG004, screening].

Limitations: the evidence does not show what determines which group runs, and about 2–3 in 100 later traces still contain both groups; the low-support lag items, though consistent, add little weight [REL015, LAG005, LAG009]. A competing explanation the evidence cannot rule out is a changed mix of case types between the windows — the later window could simply contain more cases that only ever ran one group — rather than a modified routing rule; the indicators show the behavioural difference but not what drives the choice of group [REL015, OCC001].
